strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: training deep networks with separate excitatory and inhibitory populations while avoiding batch normalization. Combining subtractive inhibition, divisive gain control, initialization, and gradient stabilization provides a coherent framework.

The reported results demonstrate feasibility across VGG-16, VGG-19, and SEW-ResNet-18 with four time steps, reaching 92.12% on CIFAR-10 and 65.53% on CIFAR-100. Improvements over the reported DANN baselines, including 3.08 percentage points on VGG-19, are encouraging.

The initialization has interpretable moment calculations under explicit assumptions. The appendix supplies derivations, STE pseudocode, and basic training hyperparameters, while the ablations provide useful evidence that inhibitory gradient scaling matters in the tested configuration.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not establish a competitive advantage under controlled conditions. Most SNN baselines use different architectures and time-step counts, without matched parameter or computational budgets. The corresponding ResNet-18 BN baseline achieves 95.57% versus 92.12%, and no CIFAR-100 BN comparison is provided. Evaluation covers only two static-image datasets and reports neither repeated-run uncertainty nor failure frequencies, despite training stability being a central claim.

The technical contribution beyond existing E-I initialization and standard optimization techniques is insufficiently isolated. Table 2 lacks a separate STE ablation, independent subtractive/divisive inhibition ablations, and a controlled spiking adaptation of the closest prior E-I method. Testing epsilon only from 1e-8 to 1e-5 does not establish the necessity of adaptive replacement. Moreover, clamped Kaiming initialization for W_EE and W_IE still reaches 85.61% versus 87.03%, weakening the claim that every component is indispensable.

The stabilization mechanism does not address the full instability it identifies. Section 4.3 replaces exact zeros but leaves arbitrarily small positive denominators unchanged, allowing large currents and reciprocal gradients. For an entirely zero sample, Algorithm 1 produces infinite replacement values rather than a finite fallback. These cases require explicit handling and validation before forward stability can be claimed.

The biological justification of the inhibitory model is incomplete. A small LIF membrane time constant does not by itself imply the ReLU spike-count approximation in Equation 7; firing remains dependent on threshold, reset dynamics, and the time constant. No comparison against explicitly spiking inhibitory neurons validates this approximation. The sample-wide minimum operation also lacks a demonstrated biological implementation, limiting the broader biological-realism claims.

Important implementation details remain unspecified: how synaptic sign constraints are maintained during SGD, what constraints apply to the trainable gains, the excitatory spike surrogate derivative, the convolutional E-I connectivity, and the layerwise initialization procedure, including treatment of real-valued image inputs. These omissions hinder reproduction and verification of Dale-law compliance. Code is only promised upon publication.

The mechanistic interpretations exceed the evidence. Batch normalization does not enforce Gaussian output distributions, so bimodality alone does not establish a fundamentally distinct computational strategy. Selected histograms and a single feature-map example cannot substantiate general claims about activated/suppressed neuronal populations or cortical computation without quantitative controls.

Comparisons do not convincingly establish competitiveness. Many literature baselines use different architectures, time steps, and training protocols. The directly reproduced CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 BN baseline achieves 95.37%, versus 92.05% for the proposed method. TinyImageNet has no comparison baseline. These limitations matter given the reported 2.3–2.5-fold training-time overhead.

The contribution beyond DANN and earlier E-I networks is insufficiently isolated. Comparing the complete method against a ReLU-based DANN changes both neuron dynamics and training procedures. A controlled comparison transferring prior initialization and stabilization methods into the same spiking backbone would better establish the contribution of E-I Init and E-I Prop.

The ablations do not support the claim that every component is indispensable. Clamped Kaiming initialization still achieves 85.61%, versus 87.03% for the complete method. There is no separate STE ablation, and fixed-epsilon comparisons cover only 1e-8 through 1e-5. Experiments on CIFAR-10/VGG-8 alone provide limited support for necessity across deeper architectures and datasets.

The stabilization mechanism does not resolve all problems identified in its motivation. Algorithm 2 replaces exact zeros but leaves arbitrarily small positive denominators unchanged. An entirely zero sample produces an infinite replacement value, with no explicit finite fallback. These cases need analysis and targeted validation before making broad stability claims.

Essential reproducibility details are missing despite the useful appendix: the spike surrogate derivative, enforcement of weight-sign constraints during optimization, positivity constraints on learned gains, and precise event preprocessing are unspecified. These choices directly affect training stability and biological constraints. Code availability is deferred until publication.

The mechanistic interpretation exceeds the evidence. Section 5.3 treats bimodal currents as evidence of a mechanism distinct from normalization, but BN does not impose Gaussianity and can preserve bimodal distributions. Histograms and a single feature-map example do not establish distinct functional neuronal populations or the broader cortical-computation claims.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: training deep SNNs with separate, sign-constrained excitatory and inhibitory pathways without batch-normalization layers.

Experiments cover five static and event-based datasets and multiple VGG/ResNet architectures. Promising results include 92.05% on CIFAR-10 with four timesteps and 77.66% on CIFAR10-DVS. The reproduced VGG-19 comparison improves over DANN by 2.65 percentage points.

Provides useful pseudocode, component ablations, gradient-scaling sensitivity experiments, and transparent measurements of training time and memory. Several reproduced comparisons include five independent runs.
weaknesses: The claimed rigorous LIF-to-ReLU reduction is incorrect (Section 3.2; Appendix D.1). The derivation applies the subthreshold steady-state solution while ignoring repeated spike resets. For constant input 2, threshold 1, zero initial/reset potential, and time constant 0.1, the stated continuous LIF dynamics produce 14 spikes in a unit interval, rather than the proposed approximation of 2. Timescale separation alone therefore does not justify the inhibitory model, undermining a central biological argument.

The stabilization mechanism does not address the full instability it motivates. Algorithm 2 replaces exact zeros but leaves arbitrarily small positive denominators unchanged. An entirely zero sample produces an infinite replacement value, with no finite fallback specified. These cases need explicit handling and stress tests before broad numerical-stability claims are justified.

Comparative evidence is insufficiently controlled. Most competing methods differ in architecture, timestep budget, or training protocol. The matched CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 BN baseline achieves 95.37%, versus 92.05% for the proposed method, while training costs increase approximately 2.3–2.5 times. TinyImageNet has no comparison baseline and is resized to 32×32, providing limited evidence for the claimed large-scale scalability.

The ablations do not establish that every component is indispensable or isolate the contribution beyond prior E-I methods. Clamped Kaiming initialization still achieves 85.61%, versus 87.03% with E-I Init. The sign-constraint ablation simultaneously changes initialization; STE and the two inhibition mechanisms are not independently ablated. Testing fixed epsilon only from 1e-8 to 1e-5 does not rule out a suitably tuned conventional stabilizer. These experiments are confined to VGG-8/CIFAR-10 without reported uncertainty.

Biological and mechanistic interpretations exceed the evidence. Initialization uses batch statistics, forward stabilization requires a sample-wide minimum, and inhibitory activity is continuous rather than explicitly spiking. These choices require qualification of the biological-realism claims. Likewise, bimodal current histograms do not demonstrate a mechanism fundamentally distinct from normalization: BN standardizes moments and does not require Gaussian outputs.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified, including the excitatory spike surrogate derivative, how nonnegative weights are maintained during optimization, constraints on the gain parameters, and the exact event-dataset splits. Code is promised only upon publication. These omissions are consequential for a method whose main contribution depends on sensitive training dynamics.
